questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The committee ______ divided in its opinion.'

options.option_text: are (wrong: 'committee' as a collective noun takes singular verb when acting as a unit; BUT here 'divided in its opinion' implies internal disagreement — still 'is' for standard British/Indian English)
is (correct: 'committee' is a collective noun; in Indian/British English, collective nouns take singular verbs when treated as a single unit ✓)
were (wrong: past tense; the sentence is in present tense)
have been (wrong: 'committee have been divided' uses plural which is American English; standard for exams = singular)

questions.explanation: B is correct. COLLECTIVE NOUNS (committee, team, jury, government, family, class) take SINGULAR verbs in Indian and British English when referring to the group as a unit. 'The committee IS divided.' In American English, plural is also acceptable, but Indian exams follow British convention: committee/jury/team = singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'Neither the students nor the teacher ______ present.'

options.option_text: are (wrong: with 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject CLOSER to the verb; 'teacher' is singular → 'is')
is (correct: 'Neither A nor B' — verb agrees with B (the subject nearer to verb); 'teacher' is singular → IS ✓)
were (wrong: past tense; sentence is in present)
have been (wrong: past perfect and plural form; doubly wrong here)

questions.explanation: B is correct. RULE: With 'Either...or' and 'Neither...nor', the verb agrees with the SUBJECT CLOSER TO THE VERB (proximity rule). '...nor the teacher' is closest → 'teacher' is singular → verb = IS. If it were '...nor the teachers' → plural → verb = ARE. This is one of the most tested SVA rules.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'The news ______ shocking.'

options.option_text: are (wrong: 'news' is always singular and uncountable; takes singular verb)
is (correct: 'news' is always singular and uncountable; 'the news IS' ✓)
were (wrong: past tense and plural; news is singular)
have been (wrong: plural and past; news takes singular present 'is')

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'NEWS' is always SINGULAR and UNCOUNTABLE — it takes singular verbs. 'The news IS good.' NOT 'the news ARE good.' Similarly uncountable singulars: information, advice, furniture, luggage, equipment, knowledge, progress, scenery — all take singular verbs.

questions.stem:
Choose the correctly agreed sentence:
A. Each of the students have submitted their assignment.
B. Each of the students has submitted his/her assignment.
C. Each of the students are submitting their assignment.
D. Each of the students were submitting their assignment.

options.option_text: A (wrong: 'each' takes singular verb; 'have' is plural)
B (correct: 'each' is always singular → takes singular verb 'has' ✓)
C (wrong: 'each' takes singular verb; 'are' is plural)
D (wrong: 'each' takes singular verb; 'were' is plural past)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'EACH', 'EVERY', 'EITHER', 'NEITHER' — these pronouns are ALWAYS SINGULAR and take singular verbs. 'Each of the students HAS submitted.' Never 'each have.' Memorise: E-E-E-N → Each, Every, Either, Neither → all take singular verbs.

questions.stem:
Identify the correct sentence:
A. The scissors is on the table.
B. Five miles are a long distance.
C. Ten years have passed since we last met.
D. The trousers was too loose for me.

options.option_text: A (wrong: 'scissors' is always plural → 'scissors ARE on the table')
B (wrong: 'five miles' as a distance measurement = singular → 'Five miles IS a long distance')
C (correct: 'ten years' as a duration of time = plural → 'ten years HAVE passed' ✓)
D (wrong: 'trousers' is always plural → 'the trousers WERE too loose')

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Ten years HAVE passed' — when years refer to a duration of time over which something happened, use plural verb. Compare: 'Ten years IS a long time' (as a single quantity/measurement = singular). 'Scissors' and 'trousers' are always plural (no singular form). 'Five miles IS far' (measured distance as single unit = singular).

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Mathematics ______ my favourite subject.'

options.option_text: are (wrong: subjects ending in '-ics' take singular verbs: mathematics, physics, economics)
is (correct: '-ics' subjects are singular; 'Mathematics IS my favourite subject' ✓)
were (wrong: past and plural; '-ics' subjects need singular present 'is')
have been (wrong: plural and past)

questions.explanation: B is correct. SUBJECTS ENDING IN '-ICS' take SINGULAR verbs: mathematics IS, physics IS, economics IS, statistics IS, politics IS, ethics IS. Exception: 'Athletics are banned' when referring to multiple events/activities (context-dependent). But as academic subjects, always singular.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct sentence:
A. A number of students was absent.
B. A number of students were absent.
C. A number of students is absent.
D. A number of student were absent.

options.option_text: A (wrong: 'a number of students' takes plural verb — 'were', not 'was')
B (correct: 'A number of + plural noun' takes PLURAL verb ✓)
C (wrong: 'is' is singular; 'a number of students' takes plural)
D (wrong: 'student' should be 'students'; and though 'were' is correct, the noun form is wrong)

questions.explanation: B is correct. RULE: 'A number of + plural noun' → PLURAL verb. 'A number of students WERE absent.' Contrast: 'THE number of students IS increasing' (the number = singular). Memory trick: 'A number' means 'some' = plural; 'The number' means one specific count = singular.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb: 'Three-fourths of the work ______ completed.'

options.option_text: are (wrong: 'work' is uncountable/singular; the fraction agrees with the noun after 'of')
is (correct: 'three-fourths of the work' — fraction + uncountable noun → singular verb 'is' ✓)
were (wrong: past tense and plural)
have been (wrong: plural and past)

questions.explanation: B is correct. RULE: With fractions + 'of', the verb agrees with the NOUN after 'of'. 'Three-fourths of the WORK' → work is uncountable → singular verb IS. 'Three-fourths of the STUDENTS' → students is plural → plural verb ARE. 'Work completed is' ✓ vs 'students... are' ✓.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'The police ______ arrested the suspect.'

options.option_text: has (wrong: 'police' is always plural in English; takes plural verb)
have (correct: 'police' is always treated as plural; 'The police HAVE arrested' ✓)
was (wrong: past singular; police is always plural)
is (wrong: present singular; police is always plural)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'POLICE' is always PLURAL — it has no singular form (one officer = a policeman/policewoman/police officer, not 'a police'). 'The police HAVE arrested...' Similarly: 'cattle' (always plural), 'people' (always plural), 'poultry' (collective, singular). 'Police' is one of the most tested words in SVA.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct sentence:
A. My spectacles needs to be cleaned.
B. My spectacles need to be cleaned.
C. My spectacle needs to be cleaned.
D. My spectacles are needed to be cleaned.

options.option_text: A (wrong: 'spectacles' is always plural → 'need', not 'needs')
B (correct: 'spectacles' is always plural → takes plural verb 'need' ✓)
C (wrong: 'spectacle' in singular means a spectacular sight, not eyeglasses)
D (wrong: 'are needed to be cleaned' is grammatically awkward; 'need to be cleaned' is the standard form)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'SPECTACLES' (eyeglasses) is always plural → takes plural verb 'need.' Note: 'spectacle' (singular) means a public show or spectacle — completely different meaning. Other always-plural words: spectacles, trousers, scissors, tweezers, pliers, goggles, tongs. All take plural verbs.
